title: miniCTX: Neural Theorem Proving with (Long-) Contexts
abstract: We introduce miniCTX, a benchmark for evaluating neural theorem provers in real-world settings where proofs depend on new context. miniCTX presents a unique challenge by requiring models to reason over long contexts and handle dependencies that arise in real-world theorem proving tasks.

sections.title: The Core Insight
sections.content: Imagine you're trying to prove a mathematical theorem. You need to understand the context, including definitions, lemmas, and comments. Context-dependent theorem proving is crucial in real-world applications. We propose miniCTX, a benchmark that evaluates neural theorem provers in this setting.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: miniCTX consists of 762 theorems from six projects, each with its own context. The model must generate a proof based on this context. We use Lean as the verifier and provide a Python wrapper for the Lean REPL.

sections.title: Benchmark Results
sections.content: We evaluate several baselines on miniCTX, including GPT-4o, state-tactic prompting, and file-tuning. The results show that context-dependent methods improve theorem proving. For example, the file-tuned model achieves 35.94% on miniCTX, outperforming the state-tactic model.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: miniCTX addresses the gap between the evaluation of current language model-based provers and the complexity of real-world theorem proving. By using real-world contexts, miniCTX drives the development of methods that understand and work with context.

sections.title: Key Innovations
sections.content: miniCTX introduces several key features, including real-world theorem proving, contextual evaluation, and automatically updating the benchmark. We also provide NTP-TOOLKIT for automated data extraction and evaluation.

sections.title: Try It Yourself
sections.content: We open-source the dataset and evaluation code for miniCTX. You can try it yourself and explore the possibilities of context-dependent theorem proving.
